summary: Registers an ENUM service for Instant Messaging, focusing on putting im: URIs into ENUM. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Look up a phone number and find the chat address for it.

subtitle: Registers an ENUM service that maps a telephone number to an im: instant messaging URI.

tldr.problem: Telephone numbers could be mapped by ENUM to presence services, but there was no enumservice for advertising instant messaging information for a number.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the enumservice im, with type im and URI scheme im:, and leaves the choice of IM protocol to the discovery mechanism in RFC 3861.
tldr.outcome: A number can resolve to an im: URI. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists RFC 6118 as updating it.

today: RFC 5028 is a Proposed Standard, and RFC 6118 is listed as updating it.

sections.title: ENUM and Instant Messaging
sections.content:
ENUM uses DNS to translate telephone numbers such as +12025550100 into URIs such as im:user@example.com. It exists primarily to connect systems that rely on telephone numbers with those that use URIs.

Instant Messaging is defined in RFC 2778. RFC 3861 defines the generic im: URI scheme. RFC 3953 already defines an enumservice for presence that returns pres: URIs, and this document adds one for IM.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone numbers can already point to presence. This adds a pointer to a chat address.

sections.title: The Registration
sections.content:
The enumservice name is im, the type is im, there are no subtypes, and the URI scheme is im:. Intended usage is COMMON and the author is Rohan Mahy.

The resource identified is an im: URI. That scheme does not name a protocol for message delivery. Instead, the mechanism in RFC 3861 is used to discover whether an IM protocol supported by the querying party is also supported by the target.
sections.plainLanguage: The entry gives a chat address but not the chat app. The two sides work out a common app afterward.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
All DNS records must be assumed to be available to all inquirers, so ENUM data is open to the public. Revealing an im: URI by itself is unlikely to cause many privacy concerns, though it might reveal a full name or employer; anonymous URIs mitigate this.

DNS offers no assurance that answers are authentic, and many problems are prevented when the resolver verifies answers with DNSSEC. The more serious concerns are attacks on the IM system itself, so any IM protocol used with im: is required to meet the requirements of RFC 2779, which call for authentication, integrity and confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can read the directory, so the chat system must protect against fakes and snooping.
